newsitem.title: MEXICO: Foreign broadcasters blacked out during Mexico vote.
newsitem.headline: Foreign broadcasters blacked out during Mexico vote.

text.p: Foreign broadcasters have had their signals blocked in Mexico to prevent viewers from seeing their coverage of the country's key mid-term elections on Sunday, cable television officials said on Saturday.

The news blackout is an effort by the pro-government Television and Radio Industry Chamber (CIRT) to ensure compliance with electoral law here that prohibits any reference to opinion polls -- even old ones -- in the week before elections.

Signals from Atlanta-based Cable News Network, British Broadcasting Corp., Microsoft and NBC's MSNBC cable channel, CBS Telenoticias, Bloomberg Information Television, and Spain's TVE were already blocked on Saturday.
In their place was a blank screen with a message from local cable television operators:

"In accordance ...with Mexican electoral law, the signal normally broadcast on this channel will be unavailable until July 7, 1997 because its content could contain material that refers to opinion polls or the preferences of Mexican voters."
In addition, signals from U.S. networks ABC, NBC and CBS were also being blocked when they carried stories on the Mexican elections, according to observers.
The CIRT blocked a CNN report on Saturday by correspondent Harris Whitbeck on the elections.
"CNN strongly believes in freedom of the press and believes it has an obligation to report fairly and honestly about the Mexican elections," CNN spokesman Steve Haworth told Reuters.

"We will continue to report on the elections, and that signal will go from Atlanta around the world. We recognise the rights of the Mexican government to legally decide how that signal will be transmitted inside Mexico," he added.
A producer from Spanish television, who did not want to be identified, told Reuters the CIRT had also blocked his outgoing transmissions from Mexico to Spain.
"I am not being allowed to work," the journalist said.

Mexican cable network CNI Canal 40 told Reuters it had blocked CBS Telenoticias for much of Saturday, but would resume transmissions after reaching an agreement with the network on scrapping all references to polls.
Mexican officials, including Interior Minister Emilio Chuayfett, met with the heads of Mexico's pay-TV industry on Friday to warn them about the restrictions, Reforma newspaper said on Saturday.

The restrictions have also affected newspapers and print journalists. In the past week, Mexican newspapers were unable to reprint news stories from international media that referred to recent opinion polls.
When asked by local reporters about the restrictions, President Ernesto Zedillo defended the blackout.
"How would you all feel if you complied with the law, and foreign media -- whom we respect and allow total freedom -- took advantage of local media outlets (to break the law)," he said.
Zedillo, whose PRI has held power for 68 consecutive years, has promised Sunday's election will be the cleanest in Mexico's history.
